text: What would happen if you fell into Jupiter? A real spacecraft already did, and it kept talking for fifty-eight minutes.
Jupiter is a planet with more than three hundred times the mass of Earth. And NASA says it has no true surface. So what does a fall into it even mean?
Here is the number to hold on to. The probe sent back data from a fall of one hundred fifty-six kilometres. Jupiter's radius is more than seventy-one thousand.
So the probe covered less than a quarter of one percent of the way to the centre. That is our sum. Everything below it is a model, and we will stamp it that way.
And that probe fell through a spot so dry that scientists compared it to a desert. Did it show us Jupiter, or just one strange place on it? Let's go down and find out.
First, getting in.
On the seventh of December, 1995, the probe hit the top of Jupiter's atmosphere at forty-seven point six kilometres a second. That is about a hundred and seventy thousand kilometres an hour.
Slowing down put more than two hundred times the pull of gravity on it.

For about two minutes, the air itself was the brake. Then the probe opened a parachute, and let go of its heat shield. There was no ground to hit. The only question was how long it could keep reporting.
And it did not report straight to Earth. It sent its data to the Galileo orbiter, which carried it home. Six instruments were measuring on the way down.
From here on, the dial that matters is pressure. We'll count the fall in bar, a unit of pressure, and watch the gauge climb. The first thing the probe found was a surprise.

Jupiter's clouds are usually described in three layers, which NASA says together span about seventy-one kilometres. That is less than half the distance the probe fell, though the two are not measured from the same starting height.
But the probe found only one distinct cloud structure, and it was of modest size. Even the lightning was scarce: about a tenth as often as on Earth.
The air was drier than anyone expected. The helium came out at about half of what was predicted. Heat was off too: temperatures were much higher than predicted.
NASA said the high temperatures seemed to need a heating process nobody had identified.
All of this is stamped HEARD. A real instrument was in that air. Before we explain the dryness, the probe measured something else strange.
At the cloud tops, the winds blew at about eighty to a hundred metres a second. Going down, they speeded up. Between one and four bar they rose sharply, to about one hundred seventy metres a second.
That is about six hundred and ten kilometres an hour, by our sum.
Then something odd. They stayed near that speed all the way down to twenty-one bar. The wind did not fade.
The scientists who studied the data said it was still unclear whether sunlight or heat from the inside was driving it.
Decades later, the Juno orbiter's gravity data suggested the jet streams reach about three thousand kilometres down. That is about twenty times deeper than the probe fell.
The authors estimate that moving layer holds about one percent of Jupiter's mass. The probe had only touched the top of it. NASA puts the Great Red Spot's depth at only about five hundred kilometres.
Even that storm is a thin skin on the planet.
Now the mystery. The probe found dry air. Was Jupiter dry, or was the probe unlucky? NASA's later reports from the orbiter helped.
The place the probe entered was a dry spot, a gap in the clouds through which deeper, warmer layers can be seen. Scientists said it had landed in the Sahara Desert of Jupiter.
The orbiter found that the air around such a spot holds far more water, and that dry spots cover under one percent of the atmosphere. So the probe's reading was true, and unusual.
Then came the next test. The Juno orbiter looked at the equator with microwaves, and found water at about two point seven times the Sun's oxygen-to-hydrogen ratio, with wide error bars.
The authors said the probe had entered a meteorologically anomalous site. But they also noted it is still unconfirmed whether the equator speaks for the whole planet.
Juno's radiometer looked from about seven tenths of a bar down to thirty, deeper than the probe's last reading.
The difference is that it looked from orbit, along the whole equatorial zone, instead of one dive at one spot.
So the dryness was real, and local. That is the first lesson of a single probe.

At fifty-eight minutes, pressure had reached twenty-three atmospheres. The temperature topped three hundred degrees Fahrenheit, which is about a hundred and fifty Celsius, by our conversion. The transmitters went silent.
That pressure was more than twice what the mission required. It was a good run. Then there was nothing to hear.
NASA says the probe was eventually vaporized in the deeper atmosphere. No instrument told us that. It is a model, so from here on the stamp changes.
Jupiter has no true surface. There is no floor to land on. Its average density is about one point three times that of water, so the whole planet is a bit heavier than a ball of water.
Going down, pressure and temperature rise until the hydrogen is squeezed into a liquid.
Deeper still, models say hydrogen may begin to carry electricity like a metal, which may help make Jupiter's magnetic field.
Most models include a layer of this metallic hydrogen, with helium separating out at the top of it as a kind of rain.
Nothing in this stage has ever been measured by an instrument inside it. It comes from physics, and from how Jupiter pulls on a passing spacecraft.
That pull is what Juno measured. Conventional models, with a distinct rock-and-ice core, predicted some gravity values larger than Juno saw.
Models with a dilute core, with heavy elements mixed in with the hydrogen and helium, fit better.
In the best-fit models, that dilute core reaches out to about sixty-three percent of the radius, with heavy elements at only about eighteen percent of the mass.
NASA now describes the core as larger than expected and not solid, with no clear line between it and the metallic hydrogen. That fuzzy zone starts more than twenty-six thousand kilometres down.
That is about a hundred and seventy times deeper than the probe got. Both numbers are our sums.
Let's be honest about where the data ends. A probe has been about a hundred and fifty-six kilometres in.
First, what was heard. Winds, temperature, pressure, helium, a thin cloud, and dry air, all measured by instruments until the signal ended. Even that evolved.
The first public summary, in January 1996, said winds of perhaps up to three hundred thirty miles an hour.
A reanalysis in 1997 settled on about one hundred seventy metres a second, and its cloud-top speeds agree with the images from Voyager. The numbers moved as people checked them.
Second, a single spot. This was one dry patch, at one moment, on a planet that could hold more than thirteen hundred Earths. Juno's equatorial water readings differ, and still have wide error bars.
Third, the models. They match Juno's gravity data, but different assumptions about hydrogen give different cores. The sixty-three percent is one model's best fit, not a reading.
Even NASA's own pages differ on how far the probe went. One says a hundred and fifty-six kilometres. Another says about two hundred. We used the first, because it is tied to the instruments' data.
The same goes for the last reading. Some reference sites give slightly different numbers. We used NASA's own wording, twenty-three and over three hundred Fahrenheit.
Where sources differ, we say about, and we show the range.
And so the probe's descent is known, but what it means for the whole planet is not settled.

So here's the honest answer. A real probe fell into Jupiter and talked for fifty-eight minutes. It went a hundred and fifty-six kilometres down, and heard winds that did not fade and air drier than anyone expected.
It was a single dry spot, and Juno has only started to show us how different the rest can be. Below that, the liquid, the metal and the fuzzy core are a best fit, and not a reading.
The only way to turn a model into a reading is to go there again.
If you could send one more probe, where on Jupiter would you aim it, and what would you ask it to measure?
